source.title: sudoLLM : On Multi-role Alignment of Language Models
source.authors: Soumadeep Saha; Akshay Chaturvedi; Joy Mahapatra; U. Garain

page_placements.theme: Adversarial control extends beyond harmful-request refusal

record.tranche_reason: The paper cites shallow safety alignment as motivation for testing prefix attacks, but its experiments report how those attacks perform against its own deliberately trained, role-conditioned access-control models. They do not test whether ordinary safety alignment is shallow or whether the claim holds in otherwise safety-trained models.
record.gate_note: The paper reports role-aware alignment results and prefix-attack success rates for models fine-tuned to answer Alice and refuse Bob. That refusal behavior is deliberately induced by the study's training, so it is not evidence that safety-trained models otherwise exhibit the behavior described in V1–V4. The prefix-attack results are recorded under fits_no_version as outcomes for this induced access-control setting. The paper does not measure aligned-versus-base per-token KL, weight localization, or safety deepening.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Qi et al.'s shallow-alignment result only to motivate its prefix attack. The refusals being attacked are deliberately induced, by instruction or fine-tuning, for an access-control task: refusing medical and legal queries from 'Bob'. These are not ordinary safety refusals of harmful requests. The results compare the authors' own BFT method against Inst. and VFT baselines. None of V1–V7 is tested on uninduced safety behaviour.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that sudoLLM (biased query rewriting plus fine-tuning) improves role-aware alignment, generalization and fail-closed behaviour. They report it improves prefix-attack robustness (about 13× or more for GPT-4o). They theorize that the bias signal eases the conflict between the language-modelling and safety objectives, and present the method as a complementary security layer.
record.recipe_differences: The study fine-tunes GPT-4o and GPT-4.1-mini for role-conditioned access control using biased query rewrites and answer/refusal targets. It does not reproduce the original harmful- or benign-fine-tuning method, per-token KL measurement, or safety-deepening training.
record.method_sensitivity: Attack success varies with target model (GPT-4.1-mini versus GPT-4o), training strategy (Inst., VFT, BFT), and prefix length (5–100 words). The paper says the API did not allow response pre-filling; its successful attack used an assistant prefix followed by a user request to continue.

fits_no_version.finding: A prefix-continuation attack (assistant prefix followed by a user request to continue) bypasses induced access-control refusal. For GPT-4.1-mini Inst. and VFT, ASR is about 60–92%. For GPT-4o, ASR is 7–21% with Inst. and 12–15% with VFT. BFT lowers ASR to 0.4–0.6% for GPT-4o and 23–44% for GPT-4.1-mini. ASR generally rises with prefix length for Inst.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Completion-prefix attacks bypass refusals induced by instruction or fine-tuning for role-based access control, and a role-bias signal in queries reduces this.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (Findings), accepted to EMNLP 2025
record.problems: Prefix-attack results concern the study's deliberately induced access-control behavior rather than uninduced safety behavior. The paper notes that its datasets are not highly curated, experiments use API-based models and smaller open models due to hardware limits, and results may change with much larger fine-tuning datasets. It states that attack results are averaged across three sets of completion prefixes and reports standard deviations.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted from Table 4 or the separately stated 93.3% Alice-BQ attack result. Other access-control alignment and adversarial-detection results were not extracted because they do not measure any listed claim version or directly bear on the prefix-attack outcome.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples of a safety-trained model.
No measurement of benign fine-tuning eroding ordinary safety. VFT/BFT train refusal for a custom task, not harmful compliance.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
Prefix-continuation attacks target only instruction- or fine-tuning-induced refusal of medical/legal queries, not ordinary refusal of harmful requests.
There is a speculative discussion of tension between the language-modelling and safety objectives, but no test of a cause.
No training aimed at deepening safety beyond the first tokens. BFT is a role-signal method and was not evaluated as a deepening method.

record.verdict_notes: The OpenAI API disallowed prefilling, so the attack places the prefix in an assistant turn followed by a user request to continue. Refusal was judged by DeepSeek-V3. The medical/legal 'unsafe' topics are stand-ins chosen because of terms of service, not harmful requests.

versions.untested_parts: No test of harmful-example fine-tuning causing ordinary safety-trained models to comply.
No test of benign fine-tuning eroding ordinary safety behavior.
No per-token KL measurement between aligned and base models.
Prefix attacks are evaluated only against deliberately role-conditioned access-control models, not as a test of ordinary safety-trained models.
No test of safety being localized in a small set of weights or ranks.
No test of whether data or objective causes safety shallowness.
No training to deepen safety or evaluation of whether deepened safety holds up.

rows.operation_detail: Repeated prefix attack using Alice's biased query instead of Bob's

conditions.value: Alice BQ; comparison stated against Bob BQ and Inst.

rows.note: Reported as a discussion comparison for the study's role-conditioned BFT model.
rows.check: This is a sanity check: an attack using Alice's authorised query wording (93.3%) against the BFT GPT-4o model. It shows the model keys on the bias signal, not anything about shallow safety. State 'partial' is meaningless here.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: The study operationally uses completion-prefix attacks motivated by shallow alignment, while evaluating induced role-conditioned refusals rather than testing ordinary harmful-request safety alignment.

tranche.reason: Section 4.3 uses shallow alignment to motivate an attack and reports its own access-control method's robustness. The medical/legal refusals are deliberately induced through instructions or role-aware fine-tuning; these results do not test a claim version under the verdict rules.

source_check.notes: Table 4 reports means and standard deviations across three completion-prefix sets; its prefix-length header specifies words although surrounding prose says tokens. Appendix B identifies gpt-4o-2024-08-06 and gpt-4.1-mini-2025-04-14, with DeepSeek V3 judging refusals.
